payload.note: Contact-quotient's canonical computation uses the electroglottographic (EGG) signal: the contact phase is extracted from the EGG waveform via derivative zero crossings, and the quotient is the contact-phase duration divided by T0. The definition states the signal source is 'the electroglottographic or glottal-flow signal', but EGG is the primary modality — it is the direct measurement of vocal-fold contact that the parameter quantifies. Removing electroglottography as a capability would eliminate the direct measurement modality for this parameter; the parameter would lose its primary operational definition and relegate itself to an indirect glottal-flow approximation.

payload.name: glottal-flow-declination-rate
payload.scope: A human-made voice-quality measurement parameter quantifying the steepest negative slope of the glottal airflow pulse within the glottal cycle (the maximum flow declination), built to persist as a standardized clinical parameter of the glottal source parameter set in speech science and laryngology.

definition.body: The glottal flow declination rate (GFD) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the steepest negative slope of the glottal airflow pulse within each glottal cycle: the maximum magnitude of the falling (negative) portion of the first derivative of the glottal flow, a measure of how abruptly the vocal folds close. Given the glottal flow waveform g(n) (the glottogram) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, GFD is computed per pitch-synchronous cycle as max(-g'(n)) over the samples where g'(n) is negative (the first difference or finite difference of g within the cycle, clipped at zero), then aggregated across cycles by the median or mean over the analyzed voiced frames. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal flow waveform g(n) - the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, the sole operand, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, which frames the per-cycle window, (3) the derivative operator - first difference or finite difference over the sampled flow, (4) the directional selection - the negative (declination) branch of the derivative only, (5) the cross-cycle aggregation (median or mean). A high GFD marks an abrupt glottal closure (pressed, spiky phonation); a low GFD marks a gradual, incomplete closure (breathy, hyperfunctional phonation), with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. It is reported in standardized units and persists as a member of the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits, documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology (the Dewaele glottal-source parameter set), and maintained alongside the maximum flow derivative, the glottal closure instant, the phase quotients, jitter, and shimmer. e.g.: GFD reported per frame in a laryngeal muscle-tension dysphonia study; GFD of a creaky-voice glottogram in a voice-disorder case report; GFD computed from an EGG-based glottogram in a pressed-phonation assessment | not: maximum flow derivative MFD (max magnitude of g' in both directions); return phase (a duration, not a slope) [formal: declivitas fluminis glottidis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: apq1
payload.scope: To standardize the measurement of period instability in voiced speech for diagnosing voice disorders in clinical laryngology and speech science.

definition.body: APQ1 (average absolute difference) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the average absolute difference of the fundamental period between consecutive glottal cycles in a voiced speech signal. For N consecutive glottal cycles with periods P_i, the perturbation is computed as APQ1 = (1/(N-1)) * Σ_i |P_{i+1} - P_i| / ((1/N) * Σ_i P_i), reported in percent or in absolute units (milliseconds or seconds). Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal segmented at pitch-synchronous cycle boundaries, (2) the per-cycle fundamental period measure. Small APQ1 indicates period stability (normal phonation); large APQ1 indicates period instability (dysphonia). Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by acoustic analysis software (Praat, laryngology toolkits) from pitch-synchronous period tracks; it persists as a documented measurement in voice-disorder assessment. e.g.: Praat's jitter analysis reporting the APQ1 value; the Kay Bolt Multi-Dimensional Voice Analysis software displaying APQ1 in its voice-quality report | not: jitter (the general category of period perturbation, not the specific APQ1 computation); shimmer (an amplitude perturbation parameter, not a period perturbation) [formal: titubatio quotiens media absoluta | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: apq3

definition.body: APQ3 (average absolute difference of amplitude) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the average absolute difference of the per-cycle amplitude between consecutive glottal cycles in a voiced speech signal. payload.name: jrr
payload.scope: To standardize the measurement of period ratio instability in voiced speech for diagnosing voice disorders in clinical laryngology and speech science.

definition.body: JRR (jitter ratio, also called J-RAP) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the ratio of the average absolute difference of the fundamental period between consecutive glottal cycles to the mean of the fundamental period, reported as a percentage. For N consecutive glottal cycles with periods P_i, the jitter ratio is computed as JRR = mean(|P_{i+1} - P_i|) / mean(P_i) * 100, where mean is over the N-1 consecutive pairs and the denominator mean is over all N periods. Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal segmented at pitch-synchronous cycle boundaries, (2) the per-cycle fundamental period measure. Small JRR indicates period stability (normal phonation); large JRR indicates period instability (dysphonia). Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by acoustic analysis software (Praat, MDVP) from pitch-synchronous period tracks; it persists as a documented measurement in voice-disorder assessment and is reported alongside APQ1 and JDP in the jitter analysis family. e.g.: JRR value displayed in the Kay Bolt MDVP jitter analysis report; JRR computed from a sustained /a/ vowel in the GRBAS voice assessment protocol; JRR reported in the acoustic analysis of dysphonia severity in laryngology research | not: APQ1 (normalized absolute difference, different formula); JDP (absolute difference as percent, different formula); shimmer (amplitude, not period) [formal: titubatio rapport | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: jdp

definition.body: JDP (jitter difference period, also called absolute jitter or abs-jitter) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the absolute average of the consecutive fundamental-period differences, expressed in time units (typically microseconds or milliseconds), computed as the mean of |P_{i+1} - P_i| over N-1 consecutive glottal cycles. payload.name: grbas
payload.scope: A human-made standardized perceptual voice-rating scale, built so that a trained rater's judgment of a voice sample is scored consistently across clinics and studies, persisting as the perceptual arm of voice-disorder assessment.

definition.body: GRBAS (the Grossman scale of roughness, breathiness, asthenia and strain, with a gross pathologic rating) is a standardized perceptual voice-rating scale scoring a voice sample on five dimensions: G - gross pathologic rating (0 none, 1 minimal, 2 moderate, 3 severe voice disorder), R - roughness (non-periodic vibration, 0 none to 3 severe), B - breathiness (excessive airflow, 0 none to 3 severe), A - asthenia (weakness of loudness, 0 none to 3 severe), S - strain (harsh tight quality, 0 none to 3 severe). Each dimension is rated on an ordinal 4-point scale by a trained rater listening to the sample, typically a sustained /a/ vowel, and the total score runs 0 to 15. Parameters: (1) the speech sample, typically a sustained /a/ vowel recorded from the patient, (2) the five maintained perceptual dimensions with their anchor descriptors, (3) the 0-3 ordinal rating per dimension, (4) the 0-15 total score. A higher total score indicates a more severe perceptual voice disorder. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical scale maintained by the discipline of laryngology and speech-language pathology - taught in voice-disorder curricula, used in research protocols comparing treatment outcomes, and implemented in voice-assessment software; it persists as the maintained perceptual counterpart of the acoustic parameter set in voice-disorder assessment. e.g.: GRBAS total score of 11/15 reported in a vocal-fold nodule surgery outcome study; GRBAS roughness (R) subscale rating of a post-laryngectomy voice in a voice-rehabilitation case report; a three-rater GRBAS panel scoring a sustained /a/ sample in a laryngology research protocol | not: a Kay Bolt MDVP jitter report (an instrumental acoustic computation, not a rater judgment); the VHI-10 voice handicap index (a patient self-report questionnaire, not a trained-rater scale); glottal flow declination rate (a computed derivative of the glottogram, not a perceptual dimension) [formal: ratio qualitatif vocis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.note: Contact-quotient operates on the electroglottographic or glottal-flow signal — its definition states parameters include 'the electroglottographic or glottal-flow signal estimated per voiced frame.' Without the glottal-flow waveform (the Cn computation needs the contact phase from g(n)), Cn cannot be computed. The removal test: remove glottal-flow now and contact-quotient stops operating. This mirrors closure-quotient and open-quotient which both hold accepted DEPENDS_ON to glottal-flow.

Contact-quotient requires the fundamental period T0 to define the contact phase as a fraction of the period (Cn = contact phase / T0). Without pitch-estimation, T0 is unknown and the quotient cannot be computed. This follows the same pattern as closure-quotient and open-quotient, both of which hold accepted DEPENDS_ON to pitch-estimation.

payload.name: jitter-ratio
payload.scope: A human-made voice-quality parameter quantifying the relative spread of consecutive fundamental periods in voiced speech, built to persist as the ratio variant of the standardized period-perturbation (jitter) measure in voice-disorder assessment.

definition.body: Jitter ratio (JRR) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the relative spread of the fundamental period between consecutive glottal cycles: the standard deviation of the per-cycle periods divided by their mean, reported in percent. For N consecutive glottal cycles with periods P_i, JRR = (sigma(P) / ((1/N) * sum_i P_i)) * 100, where sigma(P) is the standard deviation of the periods over the N cycles. Its parameters are: (1) the voiced speech signal segmented at pitch-synchronous cycle boundaries, (2) the per-cycle fundamental period measure from pitch tracking, (3) the cross-cycle aggregation (standard deviation over mean period). A small JRR indicates period stability (normal phonation); a large JRR indicates period instability (dysphonia). It is reported in standardized units and persists as a member of the jitter analysis family in voice-disorder assessment: computed by acoustic analysis software (Kay Bolt MDVP, laryngology toolkits) from pitch-synchronous period tracks, and reported alongside APQ1 and JDP in the jitter analysis. e.g.: JRR displayed in the Kay Bolt MDVP jitter analysis report; JRR computed from a sustained /a/ vowel in the GRBAS voice assessment protocol; JRR reported in the acoustic analysis of laryngectomy or dysphonia research | not: APQ1 (average absolute difference, a different formula on the same periods); JDP (absolute difference, unnormalized time units); shimmer (amplitude perturbation, not period) [formal: ratio temporis tremoris | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: glottal-inertia-quotient
payload.scope: A human-made voice-quality parameter quantifying the shape of the glottal area cycle by the ratio of its first to zeroth moment, built to persist as a standardized clinical index of phonatory type (creaky versus breathy voice) in voice-disorder assessment.

definition.body: The glottal inertia quotient (GIQ) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the shape of the glottal area cycle: the ratio of the first to the zeroth moment of the glottal area waveform A(t) within each glottal cycle, GIQ = I1 / I0, where I_k = the integral of (t/T0)^k * A(t) dt over the cycle window T0. A high GIQ marks a late, sharply peaked area cycle (creaky voice, lobe formation); a low GIQ marks an early, rounded area cycle (breathy, hyperfunctional phonation), with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal area waveform A(t) per voiced frame - estimated from the electroglottographic signal derivative or from the glottal-flow waveform through a glottal-area model, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, which frames the cycle window and normalizes the moment integrals, (3) the moment order (first over zeroth). It is reported as a dimensionless ratio and persists as a member of the glottal-source parameter set in voice-disorder assessment: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits (Kay Elite, laryngology suites), documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology (the Dewaele glottal-source parameter set), and maintained alongside the maximum flow derivative, the glottal closure instant, and the phase quotients. e.g.: GIQ computed from an EGG-derived glottal area waveform in a creaky-voice case report; GIQ reported in a laryngology study of muscle-tension dysphonia; GIQ of a sustained /a/ vowel in a voice-disorder cohort analysis | not: contact quotient (a phase-duration fraction of T0, not a moment of the area cycle); glottal closure instant (a time point, not a shape ratio) [formal: quota inertiae glottidis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: glottal-area-function
payload.scope: A human-made glottal-geometry measurement construct quantifying the time-varying cross-sectional area of the glottal aperture across the glottal cycle, built to persist as the geometric base waveform of the area-quotient family (open, closed, contact, and area-moment quotients) in speech science and laryngology.

definition.body: The glottal area function A(t) is a voice-quality measurement construct quantifying the time-varying cross-sectional area of the glottal aperture as a function of time within the glottal cycle: the geometric area of the glottal gap A(t) between the vocal folds, normalized to the cycle's maximum area A_max, reported per cycle and aggregated over voiced frames. From the frame-aligned glottal cycle, A(t) is the area of the aperture at each phase of the cycle, and it is the geometric base operand of the area-quotient family: the open quotient (fraction of the cycle the glottis is open), the closed or contact quotient (fraction in contact), and the area-moment quotients (ratios of time-weighted moments of A(t)) are all read from A(t). Its parameters are: (1) the glottal cross-sectional area A(t) - the geometric aperture, the sole operand, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, which frames the per-cycle window, (3) the estimation route - high-speed glottography (direct imaging of the fold surfaces), electroglottography-derived area (via a calibration or area-velocity model), or inverse recovery from the glottal flow g(n) through an area-velocity model (g(t) is approximately A(t) times the local flow velocity), (4) the normalization - area relative to the cycle's maximum area A_max, and (5) the cross-cycle aggregation (median or mean over the analyzed voiced frames). A symmetric A(t) with a balanced open phase marks normal phonation; a reduced peak or skewed A(t) marks pressed or breathy phonation, with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. It is reported as a normalized area waveform and persists as the geometric base of the area-quotient family in the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits, documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology (the area-quotient literature and the glottal area-velocity models), and maintained alongside the open, closed, and contact quotients and the area-moment quotients. e.g.: glottal area function A(t) from high-speed glottography in a muscle-tension dysphonia study; glottal area function recovered from the EGG via the Shujman area-velocity model in a pressed-phonation assessment; normalized area function A(t)/A_max underlying the open-quotient computation in a sustained /a/ vowel | not: glottal flow g(t) (aerodynamic volume flow, not geometric area); electroglottography (the measurement technique, not the area waveform it estimates) [formal: functio areae glottidis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: area-velocity-model
payload.scope: A human-made computational model in speech science that relates glottal flow to glottal area through a first-order velocity equation, built to persist as a standard inference method for reconstructing the glottal area waveform from inverse-filtered glottal flow data.

definition.body: The area-velocity model is a speech-science computational construct that estimates the glottal cross-sectional area waveform A(t) from the inverse-filtered glottal-flow signal g(n) using a first-order differential relationship between area and flow velocity. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and a local flow velocity estimate v, the model computes A(t) = g(n) / v(t), where v is the characteristic velocity of airflow through the glottal aperture, parameterized by the estimated glottal area at a reference point (typically the open quotient peak) and the assumed flow regime (incompressible, quasi-steady). Its parameters are: (1) the glottal-flow waveform g(n) - the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, the primary operand, (2) the local flow velocity v(t) - a parameterized estimate of airflow velocity through the glottis, (3) the reference area A_ref - the glottal area at a known point (e.g., maximum opening), used to calibrate the velocity parameter, (4) the flow-regime assumption - incompressible, quasi-steady flow, (5) the reconstruction route - direct division or iterative optimization over the pitch-synchronous cycle. A well-calibrated area-velocity model yields a physically consistent A(t) waveform suitable for deriving the area-quotient family (open, closed, contact quotients). It is reported as the estimated area waveform per cycle and persists as a standard inference method in voice-analysis toolkits, documented in the glottal area-velocity literature (e.g., the Shujman model, Alku area-velocity method), and maintained as part of the glottal source analysis pipeline. e.g.: the Shujman area-velocity model implemented in the Praat AreaVel plugin; the Alku area-velocity method as described in Alku et al. 1996 Journal of the Acoustical Society of America; the area-velocity reconstruction in the VoiceSaw glottal source analysis toolkit | not: glottal flow g(n) (the raw waveform the model takes as input, not the area estimate); inverse filtering (the preprocessing step before the area-velocity model receives its input) [formal: modelus areae velocitatis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: jitter-rap
payload.scope: A human-made voice-quality measurement parameter quantifying the relative average of second-order period differences between consecutive glottal cycles in voiced speech, built to persist as a standardized clinical parameter for period instability assessment in laryngology and speech science.

definition.body: Jitter RAP (relative average perturbation) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the relative average of second-order cycle-to-cycle period differences, computed as the mean absolute value of the second difference of consecutive pitch periods divided by the mean pitch period, expressed in percent. For N consecutive glottal cycles with periods P_i, RAP equals the sum over i from 2 to N-1 of the absolute value of P_{i+1} minus 2 times P_i plus P_{i-1}, divided by N minus 2, all divided by the mean of all P_i. Parameters: the voiced speech signal segmented at pitch-synchronous cycle boundaries, and the per-cycle fundamental period from pitch tracking. Small RAP indicates smooth, stable period progression (normal phonation); large RAP indicates erratic period changes (dysphonia). Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by acoustic analysis software from pitch-synchronous period tracks; it persists as a documented measurement in voice-disorder assessment and clinical voice analysis reports. e.g.: The RAP jitter value displayed in the Kay Bolt MDVP jitter analysis report panel; RAP computed from sustained vowel phonation in the GRBAS voice assessment protocol using MDVP software; RAP reported in the acoustic analysis of dysphonia severity in the laryngology literature by Dewaele et al. | not: APQ1 using first-order average absolute difference; JRR the jitter ratio using simple cycle-to-cycle difference; shimmer using amplitude perturbation rather than period perturbation [formal: titubatio relativa | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: phonation-threshold-pressure
payload.scope: A human-made laryngeal voice-quality parameter that quantifies the minimum subglottal pressure required to initiate vocal-fold vibration, built to persist as a standardized clinical and experimental measure of vocal-fold load and laryngeal biomechanics in laryngology and speech science.

definition.body: The phonation threshold pressure (PTP) is a laryngeal voice-quality parameter quantifying the minimum subglottal pressure at which vocal-fold vibration begins. It is measured by ramping the subglottal pressure (or driving flow) upward through a pressure transducer — a catheter below the glottis in vivo, or a pressure line in an excised-laryx or in-vitro laryx rig — and reading the pressure value at the onset of sustained vocal-fold oscillation, reported in cmH2O or kPa. A high PTP indicates increased vocal-fold load or stiffness (hyperfunctional phonation, edema, paresis with compensatory effort); a low PTP indicates low fold tension or hypofunction. Its parameters are: (1) the measurement setup — in-vivo catheter, excised-laryx rig, or in-vitro laryx model; (2) the pressure ramp rate and the threshold criterion (first sustained oscillation of the glottal flow or fold vibration); (3) the vocal-fold state (tension, adduction, mass) the ramp is applied to; (4) the pressure reference and reporting unit. It is distinct from the subglottal pressure SGP, which is the steady-state or cycle-averaged pressure measured during ongoing phonation, while PTP is the threshold at the onset of phonation. It persists as a standardized clinical and experimental parameter documented in laryngology and voice-surgery literature, and maintained as a member of the voice-quality measurement map. e.g.: phonation threshold pressure measured by a pressure ramp in an excised-laryx study of vocal-fold stiffness; phonation threshold pressure reported in a cadaveric larynx biomechanics study comparing fold tension levels; phonation threshold pressure recorded in an in-vivo laryngeal-effort assessment using a nasotracheal catheter | not: subglottal pressure SGP (the steady-state pressure during ongoing phonation, not the onset threshold); glottal flow waveform g(t) (the output of phonation, not its onset pressure); sound-pressure level at the glottis [formal: limen pressio subglottalis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: maximum-phonation-time
payload.scope: A standardized clinical screen for voice disorders that people made to separate laryngeal (vocal-fold) pathology from respiratory-support insufficiency in a single timed sustained-phonation measure.

definition.body: Maximum phonation time (MPT) is the voice-quality parameter measuring the longest duration a person can sustain a comfortable phonation, reported in seconds: the patient takes a deep breath and phonates a comfortable-pitch /a/ (or a comfortable syllable such as /pa/) for as long as possible, and the examiner times the total voiced duration with a stopwatch from voice onset to voice offset, including any breaks in the phonation. Its parameters are: (1) the task and prompt — a single maximal breath, comfortable pitch, sustained /a/ or /pa/, (2) the timing method — total wall-clock duration of the phonation, including pauses, (3) the reference range maintained by the discipline — about 15-17 s in healthy adults, with shorter times flagging either vocal-fold pathology or reduced respiratory support, and re-measurements that isolate the two. It is reported in seconds and persists as a member of the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in laryngology suites and voice-screening checklists, taught in speech-language pathology curricula, and maintained alongside the GRBAS scale, jitter, shimmer, and the perturbation and phase quotients. e.g.: the MPT recorded as 8.4 s for a laryngectomized patient in a laryngology clinic intake; the MPT value of 12.1 s in a voice-disorder screening report for a teacher with vocal fatigue; the MPT baseline of 16.5 s maintained in a pre-treatment voice-assessment battery for a singer with vocal nodules | not: glottal-flow waveform duration (a per-cycle quantity); jitter (period perturbation, a relative measure); subglottal pressure (a transducer-measured pressure, not a timed duration) [formal: tempus phonationis maximum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: creaky-voice
payload.scope: A human-made classification category made by laryngology and speech science to name the low-frequency implosive vibration mode of phonation so it can be told apart from modal phonation in clinical assessment and voice training.

definition.body: Creaky voice (vocal fry) is a classification category for a mode of voiced phonation defined by a specific glottal configuration: the vocal folds are adducted with loose medial contact and low subglottal pressure, vibrating at a low fundamental frequency (typically well below the modal range) in an aperiodic, implosive cycle in which glottal flow falls to zero and briefly reverses near cycle end, producing a sawtooth-like flow waveform and the audible creak or fry sound. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal configuration — medial adduction with loose contact and reduced subglottal pressure, (2) the cycle signature — low f0, aperiodic implosive cycles with flow reversal, (3) the acoustic signature — a low, creaky, grainy timbre with a sparse, weakly harmonic structure. It persists as a named mode of the phonation-mode taxonomy: documented in laryngology and phonetics, used in voice-disorder assessment (creaky voice as a compensatory or pathological voice quality) and in voice training (vocal fry contrasted with modal voice), and maintained alongside the other voice modes. e.g.: the vocal fry mode at the ends of utterances in casual American English, labeled in phonetic transcription; the vocal fry category in Sundberg's five-mode phonation inventory; the creaky voice quality labeled in a laryngology report for a patient with a strained low-pitched voice | not: breathy voice (incomplete closure with modal-frequency vibration and turbulent noise leakage); modal phonation (the normal periodic mode, a different mode of the same taxonomy); whisper voice (unvoiced glottal airflow, outside voiced phonation) [formal: vox crepitans | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

Its parameters are: (1) the glottal configuration — medial adduction with loose contact and reduced subglottal pressure, (2) the cycle signature — low f0, aperiodic implosive cycles with flow reversal, (3) the acoustic signature — a low, creaky, grainy timbre with a sparse, weakly harmonic structure. It persists as a named mode of the phonation-mode taxonomy: documented in laryngology and phonetics, used in voice-disorder assessment (creaky voice as a compensatory or pathological voice quality) and in voice training (vocal fry contrasted with modal voice), and maintained alongside the other voice modes. e.g.: the vocal fry mode at the ends of utterances in casual American English, labeled in phonetic transcription; the vocal fry category in Sundberg's five-mode phonation inventory; the creaky voice quality labeled in a laryngology report for a patient with a strained low-pitched voice | not: breathy voice (incomplete closure with modal-frequency vibration and turbulent noise leakage); modal phonation (the normal periodic mode, a different mode of the same taxonomy); whisper voice (unvoiced glottal airflow, outside voiced phonation) [formal: vox crepitans | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

definition.body: Breathy voice (breathy phonation) is a classification category for a mode of voiced phonation defined by a specific glottal configuration: the vocal folds vibrate periodically at a normal fundamental frequency, but the glottis does not fully close during each cycle, so turbulent air leaks through the residual gap and adds noise to the harmonic signal, producing an audible breathy or airy timbre. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal configuration — incomplete medial closure during the vibration cycle, (2) the cycle signature — modal f0 with a shortened closed phase (a low closure quotient) and a turbulent noise leak, (3) the acoustic signature — a breathy timbre with reduced harmonic-to-noise contrast. It persists as a named mode of the phonation-mode taxonomy: documented in laryngology and phonetics, used in voice-disorder assessment (breathy voice in vocal fold paresis, as a habitual voice quality, or after laryngeal surgery) and in voice training (breathy quality contrasted with modal voice), and maintained alongside the other voice modes. e.g.: the breathy voice quality labeled in a voice-disorder assessment of a teacher with a vocal fold nodule; the breathy category in Sundberg's five-mode phonation inventory; the breathy voice quality labeled in a laryngology report for a patient with left vocal fold paresis | not: creaky voice (low-frequency aperiodic implosive vibration, a different mode); whisper voice (unvoiced glottal airflow, outside voiced phonation); modal phonation (complete glottal closure each cycle, a different mode) [formal: vox aspera | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]
